title: Why are there seasons?
subtitle: Earth & Sun
subject: sciences
description: The seasons do not come from Earth being closer to or farther from the Sun. The real cause is the tilt of Earth's axis.

hero.hook: No, summer does not arrive because Earth moves closer to the Sun.

blocks.text: Many people think summer comes when Earth is **closer** to the Sun, and winter when it is **farther** away. That is wrong. And you can see it right away: when it is summer in France, it is winter in Australia.
The real explanation comes down to one thing: Earth's axis of rotation is **tilted**, leaning relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.

Earth spins on itself in **24 hours**, which gives us day and night. It also travels around the Sun in **one year**, on an orbit shaped like an **ellipse**, a slightly flattened circle. But its axis, the imaginary line from the North Pole to the South Pole, is not perpendicular to that orbit. It leans by about **23.5 degrees**, and that is [[Earth's axial tilt (23.5°)]].

blocks.caption: The tilt of Earth's axis explains the cycle of the seasons

blocks.text: The tilt keeps pointing in roughly the same direction all year. It always aims at the same patch of sky, near the North Star. The result: depending on where Earth sits on its orbit, one hemisphere “faces” the Sun more and the other less.

In summer in the northern hemisphere, the North Pole leans toward the Sun. The days grow longer: the **photoperiod**, the ratio between the length of day and night, goes up. The rays also hit the ground more “head-on,” so the energy is packed into a smaller area. That is why it gets hotter.

In January, Earth is in fact a little **closer** to the Sun than in July. That point is the **perihelion**, the nearest point of the orbit. And yet January is winter in the north. Proof that distance does not explain the seasons.

In winter it is the reverse: short days, more slanted rays, energy spread over a larger area. Less heat received. The **solstices**, the moments when the Sun reaches its northernmost or southernmost position, mark the start of summer or winter.

Near the **equator**, the imaginary line that splits Earth into two hemispheres, the tilt barely changes the length of the day. There are not really four seasons as in Europe, but rather drier and wetter periods.
At the **poles**, the effect is extreme: several months of continuous daylight in summer, several months of night in winter. The contrast there is far sharper than in France.

If Earth's axis stood perfectly straight, every place would get roughly the same amount of sunlight all year. No real summer, no real winter. Climate, crops, animal migrations: everything would be different.
The seasons come from the **tilt** of Earth's axis, about **23.5°**, not from the distance to the Sun. One hemisphere leans toward the Sun: that is summer. The other leans away: that is winter.
